title: Best Sources of Healthy Fats: What to Eat and What They Replace

seo.title: Best Sources of Healthy Fats
seo.meta_description: Olive oil, nuts, seeds, avocado and fatty fish provide unsaturated fats. Compare realistic servings and learn why substitution matters.
seo.search_intent: Identify foods rich in unsaturated fats and use them in a heart-healthy eating pattern.

excerpt: Olive oil, nuts, seeds, avocado and fatty fish are useful sources of unsaturated fat. Their biggest advantage comes when they replace butter, fatty meats and other major sources of saturated fat.
content_html:
“Healthy fats” usually means foods rich in monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats. The goal is not to add unlimited fat to the diet. The strongest guidance focuses on replacing saturated fats with unsaturated fats while keeping total calories appropriate.

Practical sources of unsaturated fat

FoodServingApprox. fatWhat else it provides
Extra-virgin olive oil1 tbsp / 14 g14 gMostly monounsaturated fat, polyphenols
Almonds1 oz / 28 g14 gProtein, fiber, vitamin E, magnesium
Walnuts1 oz / 28 g18.5 g2.6 g ALA, protein, fiber
Avocado100 g / 3.5 oz14.7 g6.7 g fiber, potassium
Cooked salmon3 oz / 85 g~10 g~22 g protein, EPA and DHA
Chia seeds1 oz / 28 g~9 g5.1 g ALA, fiber

Olive oil

Olive oil is almost pure fat, so one tablespoon has about 120 calories. Most of its fat is oleic acid, a monounsaturated fatty acid.

Its advantage is clearest when it replaces butter or other saturated-fat-rich cooking fats. A tablespoon of butter and a tablespoon of oil are both calorie-dense, but their fatty-acid profiles differ substantially.

Nuts

Almonds, pistachios, hazelnuts and walnuts combine unsaturated fat with protein and fiber. One ounce of almonds provides about 14 g fat, 6 g protein and 3.5 g fiber.

Walnuts stand out for ALA omega-3: about 2.6 g per ounce, compared with very little ALA in almonds.

Seeds

Chia and flax are concentrated ALA sources. An ounce of chia provides about 5.1 g ALA. Hemp, pumpkin, sesame and sunflower seeds provide different mixes of polyunsaturated and monounsaturated fats plus protein and minerals.

ALA is essential, but conversion to EPA and DHA is limited. Plant seeds and fatty fish therefore are not nutritionally identical omega-3 sources.

Avocado

Avocado has about 14.7 g fat and 160 calories per 100 g, mostly from monounsaturated fat. Unlike oil, it is high in water and contains 6.7 g fiber.

Olive oil is about 884 calories per 100 g, more than five times avocado's 160, because oil is essentially all fat and avocado is roughly three-quarters water.

Fatty fish

Salmon, sardines, mackerel and herring provide EPA and DHA directly. NIH data show that 3 ounces of farmed Atlantic salmon contains about 1.8 g combined EPA+DHA; Atlantic herring about 1.7 g; canned sardines about 1.2 g.

Fish also contributes complete protein, vitamin B12 and other micronutrients.

Canola, soybean and other liquid plant oils

Non-tropical liquid plant oils generally contain more unsaturated fat and less saturated fat than butter, lard, coconut oil or palm oil. Canola oil contributes monounsaturated fat plus ALA; soybean oil supplies polyunsaturated omega-6 and some ALA.

“Plant-based” does not automatically mean low in saturated fat. Coconut and palm oils are much higher in saturated fat than olive, canola, soybean or sunflower oils.

Substitution is the key idea

If a meal already contains avocado, cheese and nuts, adding several tablespoons of oil can raise calories substantially. Heart-health guidance is most meaningful when unsaturated-fat foods replace saturated-fat foods.

Olive oil can replace butter; walnuts can replace a refined snack; salmon can replace a high-saturated-fat meat entrée.

Which source is best?

There is no single winner. Olive oil is practical for cooking; nuts and seeds add fiber and minerals; avocado is less energy-dense than oil and adds fiber; fatty fish provides EPA and DHA in a form plant foods do not.

Bottom line

A strong mix includes olive or other non-tropical plant oils, nuts, seeds, avocado and fatty fish. The most important move is replacing foods high in saturated fat rather than simply adding more fat and calories.

Sources

Food values: USDA FoodData Central. Omega-3: NIH ODS. Fat replacement guidance: American Heart Association.

faq.question: What are the best healthy-fat foods?
faq.answer: Olive oil, nuts, seeds, avocado and fatty fish provide different types of unsaturated fat and complementary nutrients.

faq.question: Is olive oil lower in calories than butter?
faq.answer: Not much by weight. Both are calorie-dense fats; the meaningful difference is the much higher proportion of unsaturated fat in olive oil.

faq.question: Can chia or flax replace fish for omega-3?
faq.answer: Not completely. They provide ALA, while fish provides EPA and DHA directly. Human conversion of ALA to EPA and DHA is limited.
